title: A Non-Freaked Out, Focused Approach to the Common Core — Part 7 — Teach Character
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Stuart argues that pursuing the Common Core's demanding cognitive goals through complex texts, close reading, argument, talk and writing alone will leave teachers and students miserable unless they also teach students how to deal with difficulty itself. Drawing on Paul Tough's How Children Succeed and KIPP's character strengths, he frames grit and self-control as non-cognitive skills that are learnable habits rather than inborn traits, and that strongly predict success. He spells out KIPP's concrete indicators for grit and for work-related and interpersonal self-control, then links each to specific Common Core tasks like gritty reading of hard texts and polite, focused debate. His team in a freshman/sophomore academy teaches each strength explicitly, but he insists the real power lies in relentlessly infusing the language into daily class life, praising specific instances, and letting students feel the intrinsic rewards. He closes by urging teachers without a supportive team to simply start in their own rooms, working within rather than against their school's curriculum.
points: Stuart's provocative claim is that a rigor-only push toward the Common Core will make teachers or students hate their lives unless students are also taught how to handle difficulty.
He treats grit and self-control as teachable, practicable skills, borrowing KIPP's observable indicators so the strengths are concrete rather than vague slogans.
Explicit lessons are only the introduction; the real driver is hearing the strengths named hundreds of times a week through specific, descriptive praise and letting students feel the payoff.
He ties each strength to literacy work: below-level readers are expected to read a complex text grittily, and debaters are expected to show self-control toward opposing views.
Teachers without a like-minded team should start in their own classroom alongside the existing curriculum, since defying school policy is usually ineffective, alienating and prideful.
quotes: But here's the bold claim I'll spend this post backing up: if you aim at the Common Core goals only by doing increased text complexity, close reading, arguing, mandatory talking, and writing like crazy, you or a large amount of your students will begin to hate your/their life.

It's about reality. And the reality is that if the goals laid out in the Common Core are to be met while retaining joy in our classrooms, we had better figure out how to teach our students not just how to deal with a complex text cognitively, but also how to develop the chops for dealing with difficulty, period.

Non-cognitive skills are those things that have nothing to do with IQ but are, in fact, pretty darn good at predicting whether or not you'll be successful. By calling them skills, we're saying that, just like dribbling a soccer ball or writing your name, they can be intentionally taught and intentionally practiced and intentionally mastered.

When I give a complex text to the whole class, my below-level readers need to know that what I'm expecting is a gritty reading of the text. They may not pull out as much as their at- or above-level peers, but I expect them to focus for the duration of the reading and to finish it.

The biggest reason our kids are starting to latch onto grit and self-control is probably because they hear them mentioned hundreds of times per week between our four classes. It's become part of the fabric of our classrooms.

But if you don't have such a luxury, the key with impacting students and colleagues is to simply get started in your own room. I am NOT advocating that you completely disregard your school's curriculum and policies — seven years into my career, I've come to realize that such behavior is usually 1) ineffective, 2) alienating, and 3) foolishly prideful. (Trust a guy who's been there.)

But our students also need to know how to deal with difficulty — not only how to deal with a difficult text, but how to deal with difficulty itself. Grit and self-control aren't the only way to teach them this but, in my opinion, they are the easiest, most straightforward, least complicated way.
